datasets.family: Climate classification and climate normals (the Köppen replacement)
datasets.scaling: tavg, tmin, tmax: multiply by 0.1 to get degC (gee:scale 0.1, confirmed in STAC AND empirically -- Arusha Jan tavg raw 202 -> 20.2 C). prec: NO scaling, already mm/month (gee:scale null). Verified internally consistent: sum of Arusha monthly prec = 1086 mm exactly equals WORLDCLIM/V1/BIO bio12 = 1086.
datasets.coverage: Global land, all three test points return values. 12 images, system:index '01'..'12' (NOT 0-indexed -- toBands() gives '01_tavg'...'12_prec').
datasets.notes: RECOMMENDED PRIMARY for the Köppen replacement. Highest resolution global monthly normals readable by this project, and the only one fine enough (~1 km) to resolve Arusha's 1401 m plateau and the Salinas Valley floor vs the Gabilan Range. Caveat: the 1960-1990 baseline is now old and runs cool/dry, which is what pushes Miami to Aw and Sao Paulo to Cfb. For Tanzania this does not matter -- Arusha and Morogoro give identical codes on the 1991-2020 baseline.

datasets.family: Climate classification and climate normals (the Köppen replacement)
datasets.scaling: tmmn, tmmx: multiply by 0.1 to get degC (gee:scale 0.1 in STAC; Arusha Jan tmmx raw 281.2 -> 28.12 C). pr: NO scaling, already mm (gee:scale null). aet/pet/def scale 0.1; pdsi scale 0.01. Monthly mean temp is computed as (tmmn*0.1 + tmmx*0.1)/2 -- TerraClimate ships no tavg band.
datasets.units: tmmn/tmmx degC; pr mm/month; aet/pet/def mm; pdsi index
datasets.coverage: Global land, 804 monthly images, all three test points return values. Time range 1958-01 to 2024-12 (verified via reduceColumns on system:time_start).
datasets.temporal_range: 1958-01 to 2024-12, monthly; I build 1991-2020 normals with filterDate + calendarRange(m,m,'month').mean()
datasets.notes: RECOMMENDED SECONDARY / modern-baseline cross-check. CC0 is the cleanest licence of anything here. Gives a real 1991-2020 baseline, which fixes Miami and Sao Paulo. BUT at 4.6 km it smooths sharp gradients and gets several coastal/monsoon cities wrong that WorldClim gets right (Beijing -> BSk, Kano -> Aw, Mumbai -> Aw, Kampala -> Am). Use it to corroborate, not as the sole source. It agrees with WorldClim at all three CropUp test points.

datasets.family: Climate classification and climate normals (the Köppen replacement)
datasets.scaling: Temperature bios (bio01, bio02, bio05-bio11): multiply by 0.1 -> degC. bio04 (temperature seasonality): multiply by 0.01. bio03 and bio15: NO scaling (percent / CV). All precipitation bios (bio12, bio13, bio14, bio16-bio19): NO scaling, already mm. Verified: Arusha bio01 raw 191 -> 19.1 C, which equals the mean of the 12 scaled WORLDCLIM/V1/MONTHLY tavg values (19.14).
datasets.units: bio01-02,05-11 degC; bio03 %; bio04 degC; bio12-14,16-19 mm; bio15 CV
datasets.coverage: Global land, all three test points return values.
datasets.notes: Not needed for the Köppen calculation itself (the monthly collection carries everything), but these 19 variables are the standard predictor set for species/crop suitability models -- directly relevant to replacing the absent 80 MB data/maxent_suitability.db. bio14 (driest-month precip) and bio12 (annual precip) are exactly the two inputs the Köppen A-branch needs, so this is a useful one-getInfo sanity check on the monthly path.

datasets.family: Climate classification and climate normals (the Köppen replacement)
datasets.scaling: NO scaling, values are already mm/day (gee:scale null, gee:units 'mm/d'). Sum daily images over a year for annual mm.

datasets.license: proprietary (per EE STAC). CHIRPS is distributed by UCSB/CHC as public-domain data with a request to cite Funk et al. 2015, but the STAC licence field literally says 'proprietary' -- do not assert CC0 in CropUp's attribution.
datasets.value_salinas: 288.7 mm/yr (mean annual total, 1991-2020) at the task point

Its Arusha total (1000 mm) sits between WorldClim (1097) and TerraClimate (812), so all three are mutually consistent. NOT usable as the sole Köppen input: precipitation only, no temperature, so it cannot produce the A/B/C/D/E main class on its own.

datasets.family: Climate classification and climate normals (the Köppen replacement)
datasets.scaling: temperature_2m: subtract 273.15 to get degC (stored in K, NOT a scaled integer). total_precipitation_sum: multiply by 1000 to get mm. These are the two easiest scaling mistakes in the whole family -- a raw ERA5-Land temperature of ~292 is Kelvin, not a 0.1-scaled degC, and a raw precip of 0.003 is metres/day, not mm.
datasets.units: temperature_2m in KELVIN; total_precipitation_sum in METRES
datasets.coverage: Global land. 919 images, 1950-01 to 2026-08. Readable by this project.
datasets.license: Copernicus / ECMWF licence -- free reuse with attribution, but requires the Copernicus attribution statement.
datasets.value_arusha: Not sampled at the test points in this investigation -- I verified only that the collection loads, its band list, and its time range. I am not quoting per-point values I did not read.
datasets.notes: Confirmed readable and viable as a third climate source, but I did NOT use it for the Köppen classifier and deliberately did not sample it, so treat the scaling note as documentation-derived rather than empirically confirmed here. At ~11 km it is the coarsest option and would be the worst of the three for Arusha's terrain. Its real value to CropUp is recent-conditions and soil-moisture/radiation, not climate normals.

datasets.family: Climate classification and climate normals (the Köppen replacement)
datasets.scaling: multiply by 1e-4. Stored as AI x 10000 signed integer. Arusha raw DN 5595 -> AI 0.559, which is physically plausible for a 1400 m East African plateau with ~1000 mm/yr. Classes: <0.03 hyper-arid, 0.03-0.2 arid, 0.2-0.5 semi-arid, 0.5-0.65 dry sub-humid, >0.65 humid.
datasets.coverage: Global land, all three test points return values. FROM THE GEE COMMUNITY CATALOG.

datasets.notes: The single most useful climate layer I found IN THE COMMUNITY CATALOG for this family, and it is wired into the delivered module as aridity_index(). It is a continuous water-availability measure, which is often more actionable for irrigation advice than a discrete Köppen letter. It is NOT a climate classification and cannot substitute for one. Also available as global_ai_monthly (12-image collection, same b1 band and same 1e-4 scaling).

datasets.family: Cropland extent and field context (is-this-cropland / land cover / irrigated-vs-rainfed / crop type / field polygon)
datasets.scaling: NO scaling on classification: it is literally 0 or 100 and means absent/present. Divide confidence by 100 to get a 0-1 probability. Verified against the EE STAC description: 'Each product (image) has a binary classification (0 or 100) and a confidence (0-100) band.'
datasets.units: classification = 0 or 100 (binary, NOT a percentage); confidence = 0-100 integer percent
datasets.coverage: Global, but tiled into 106 agro-ecological zones (AEZ); a point can fall inside TWO overlapping AEZ tiles (Salinas falls in aez_id 6137 AND 37176). Products are masked outside cropland, so maize/irrigation return null on non-crop pixels even where the tile exists.
datasets.value_arusha: temporarycrops: classification=0, confidence=99 -> NOT cropland at 99% confidence. maize/irrigation/wintercereals all masked (null).
datasets.value_morogoro: temporarycrops: classification=100, confidence=80 -> IS cropland. maize: classification=100, confidence=15 (present but very low confidence). irrigation (tc-maize-main): classification=0, confidence=90 -> RAINFED. wintercereals: 0, confidence=98.
datasets.value_salinas: temporarycrops: classification=0, confidence=99 -> NOT cropland. All other products masked (null). At a true Salinas Valley field (36.46,-121.41): temporarycrops=100 conf 48, irrigation=100 conf 45 -> IRRIGATED.
datasets.notes: THE single most valuable asset in this family and the only one that answers all three questions (cropland / crop type / irrigation) globally at 10 m. How to query a point: ic.filterBounds(pt).filter(ee.Filter.eq('product', P)).qualityMosaic('confidence') — qualityMosaic is required, not optional, because of the overlapping-AEZ duplication. product is one of {temporarycrops(106 imgs), irrigation(225), maize(133), wintercereals(106), springcereals(21)}; season is one of {tc-annual, tc-maize-main, tc-maize-second, tc-wintercereals, tc-springcereals}. aez_id has 106 distinct values. Note aez_group/startdate/enddate are advertised but return EMPTY arrays — do not filter on them.

datasets.notes: NOT on the original task list — I found it in the catalog and it is the best 30 m global rainfed-vs-irrigated layer. BUT its accuracy is visibly poor where I could ground-check it: in the Salinas Valley, which is almost entirely furrow/drip irrigated, LGRIP calls Chualar, Soledad and Spreckels class 3 RAINFED and only Gonzales and Castroville class 2 irrigated. Conversely it calls two rural Arusha points class 2 IRRIGATED, which is likely commission error over largely rainfed maize. Use it only as a tertiary fallback behind WorldCereal, and surface it to the farmer with a hedge.

datasets.family: Cropland extent and field context (is-this-cropland / land cover / irrigated-vs-rainfed / crop type / field polygon)
datasets.scaling: None. NO CLASS TABLE IS PUBLISHED anywhere — the docs page only says 'binary mask'. I determined it empirically: only values {1, 2} occur (frequency histogram over both an Arusha box and a Morogoro box). Cross-tabulating over a Morogoro box at 300 m, class 2 pixels are 58.5% ESA-WorldCover-cropland and average DEAF crop-probability 52.0%, while class 1 pixels are 14.1% and 37.0%. Therefore 1 = NON-cropland, 2 = CROPLAND. Anyone assuming the usual 0/1 binary will invert this layer.
datasets.coverage: Africa only. Returns null at Salinas and everywhere outside Africa.
datasets.notes: Verified positive at rural Arusha (-3.30, 36.55) = 2 Cropland, confirming the layer is live and the class mapping is right. Built by fusing four land-cover datasets per agro-ecological zone and reported to beat each individually and to match FAO statistics better.

datasets.scaling: None. Class table read directly off the EE asset property 'landcover_class_names': 0 Non-croplands, 1 Croplands Irrigation major, 2 Croplands Irrigation minor, 3 Croplands Rainfed, 4 Croplands Rainfed minor fragments, 5 Croplands Rainfed very minor fragments.

It does carry irrigation information in the class codes (1-2 irrigated, 3-5 rainfed), which is why I kept it as the third irrigation fallback. At a true Salinas Valley field (36.46,-121.41) the pin falls INSIDE exactly one polygon: CSBID 061623010094820, 3.353 ha, Monterey County, rotation 2016 Fallow/Idle -> 2017 Fallow/Idle -> 2018 Fallow/Idle -> 2019 Oats -> 2020 Dbl_Crop_Oats/Corn -> 2021 Corn -> 2022 Winter_Wheat -> 2023 Fallow/Idle.

It gives a real field boundary AND eight years of crop rotation from a single dropped pin. Practical gotcha: filterBounds(point) returns 0 when the pin lands on a field edge or a road, so fall back to filterBounds(point.buffer(250)) and sort by geometry().distance(point) — at Chualar the bare point gave 0 features and the 250 m buffer gave 4.

datasets.notes: BEST DATASET IN THIS FAMILY, but two traps. (1) TANZANIA IS SPATIALLY UNIFORM: I sampled 7 towns (Arusha, Morogoro, Mbeya, Mwanza, Dar, Kigoma, Mtwara) and every cropped pixel returns exactly 17.829893 kg N/ha for maize; the whole-Tanzania bbox min/max/mean = 0/18/11.52. Nset=4 (national statistics) there, vs Nset=5 in Iowa/Illinois where values do vary (151.1 and 188.9). So in Tanzania this is a NATIONAL CONSTANT dressed as a raster - it carries zero local information and must never be presented as 'your area's rate'. (2) 0 IS AMBIGUOUS: at the Salinas point all three nutrients read 0 while 30 km around them the maxima are 221.6 (maize), 214.7 (strawberry), 248.6 (lettuce). 0 means 'no area of this crop mapped in this 5.6 km cell', not 'farmers apply nothing'. The qual band does NOT flag this (it reads 0.78-0.93 at that same zero pixel). The Nset/P2O5set/K2Oset categorical codes (observed values 1, 4, 5) are NOT documented on the catalog page - I did not find a codebook, so do not label them.

datasets.notes: THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT DATASET FOR THE FERTILIZER QUESTIONS, because it is the only source that carries the distinction that keeps the advice safe. I pulled the authoritative column metadata from the authors' own repo (raw.githubusercontent.com/ludemannc/FUBC_1_to_9_2022/main/results/Meta_data_FUBC_1_to_9_data.csv) rather than guessing. Verbatim: N_rate_kg_ha = 'Mean application rate of nitrogen to area of crop that actually received fertilizer (see N_pc_fert for percentage of crop area where N was applied)'. Aver_N_rate_kg_ha = 'Mean application rate of nitrogen across total crop area'. N_pc_fert = 'Percentage of total crop area that received any nitrogen fertilizer'. So for Tanzanian maize the two numbers are 120 kg N/ha (what a farmer who fertilizes actually puts on, 1990) versus ~16.5-17.8 kg N/ha (the national area-average, because only 10-15% of maize land gets anything). 120 x 0.15 = 18, which is essentially exactly the NPKGRIDS raster value of 17.83 - that arithmetic agreement is the proof that the NPKGRIDS grid maps the AREA-AVERAGE concept, not a dose. In the US the gap nearly vanishes (97-100% of maize area fertilized, so 150 on-fertilized vs 157.6 across-total), which is why this trap is invisible if you only test on US data. CAVEAT: the newest Tanzania maize row is 2016 and the on-fertilized-area rates are from 1990-1997, i.e. ~30 years old.

datasets.notes: CRITICAL AND COUNTERINTUITIVE: the quality index is very nearly a GLOBAL CONSTANT per crop-ingredient, NOT a local confidence. For Corn/Glyphosate I sampled Iowa, Illinois, Arusha, Morogoro and Nairobi and got the byte-identical value 0.7568864822387695 at all five; Netherlands 0.7930; Salinas and Brazil 0 (invalid). For VegFru the value is identical at Arusha, Morogoro and Salinas. So a QI of 0.76 at Arusha does NOT mean the Tanzanian estimate is trustworthy - it is a global model-fit score for that crop-chemical combination, dominated by the USGS US survey data the model was trained on. Presenting it to a farmer as 'data confidence: 76%' would be actively misleading. Use it only to RANK chemicals or to suppress a layer entirely, never as a local reliability score.

datasets.notes: MISLABELLED BY EXPECTATION. This is NOT a map of what tillage farmers use - it is a meta-analysis database of published paired field experiments comparing no-till against conventional till. It cannot answer 'what tillage is practised near me'. It can only answer 'what happened when researchers tried no-till in trials somewhere near here'. It must never be interpolated into a surface. For CropUp its honest use is narrow: if a Tanzanian farmer asks about conservation agriculture / no-till, you can say that in 39 East African maize trials the median outcome was a 6% yield LOSS and no-till won in only about a third of them, and that the three Tanzanian trials on record are sorghum at Dodoma where two of three lost 62-66% of yield. That is a genuinely useful, genuinely cautionary answer, and it is the opposite of the usual no-till marketing. Note the trials mostly report early years after conversion (yrs_from_nt = 2 for the Kenyan set, 1-4 for Tanzania), and no-till is known to need several years before benefits appear - say so.

Measured against the FAO-56 normals it runs ~1.5-1.9x too high (Arusha 9.1 vs 4.7, Morogoro 7.3 vs 4.9, Salinas 7.1 vs 6.5 mm/day), and TerraClimate's ASCE Penman-Monteith PET for the same month agrees with FAO-56, not with ERA5 (Arusha 4.08, Morogoro 4.51, Salinas 4.75 mm/day). My first draft of get_water_status used it as the ETo denominator and reported a stress ratio of 0.175 at Arusha - i.e. it made a normally-watered field look severely stressed. TABLE: -1 nodata | 0 temperature | 1 precipitation | 2 climate variability (crop-failure recurrence) | 3 photoperiod | 4 soil base saturation | 5 coarse fragments | 6 soil pH | 7 salinity (EC) | 8 soil texture | 9 soil organic carbon | 10 sodicity (ESP) | 11 soil depth | 12 slope. EVIDENCE: (a) code 1 covers 100% of the Sahara under rainfed and 0% under irrigated — precipitation, certain; (b) code 6 pixels (maize, n=348k at 5 km) have 75% of pixels with SoilGrids pH outside 5.5-7.8 and mean maize pH-membership 37 vs 60 Africa-wide, and code 6 covers 87% of the Congo Basin where the GMD paper explicitly says maize is pH-limited — pH, strong; (c) code 9 pixels have SoilGrids SOC 0.57% vs 1.12% Africa mean, lowest of any class — organic carbon, strong; (d) code 8 for rice has sand 59.1% vs 51.8% mean and for cassava 72.6% — texture, strong; (e) code 12 pixels in the East African highlands have mean SRTM slope 5.87 deg vs 1.68 deg regional — slope, strong; (f) code 11 pixels have the highest coarse-fragment volume (26.0% vs 14.2% mean) — soil depth / rocky, moderate. CONFIDENCE: codes 0-3, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12 are well supported; codes 4, 5, 7, 10 follow the source ordering but I could not independently confirm them (base saturation and sodicity are not in SoilGrids, and code 7 essentially never occurs). Treat 4/5/7/10 as 'a soil chemical constraint' if precision matters.
